edition: Health news digest – Tuesday, 24 November 2026 – Afternoon edition

items.title: COPD Treatment Escalation Beyond Inhalers, With Brian Bizik, PA-C
items.summary: Following his talk at the 2026 GOLD International COPD Conference, PA Brian Bizik discusses when clinicians should consider escalating COPD therapy beyond maximized inhaler treatment, before patients reach end-stage disease.

items.title: Upstream Bio to Participate in Upcoming Investor Conferences (verekitug update)
items.summary: Upstream Bio says verekitug, which has been given to more than 500 participants and showed positive Phase 2 results in severe asthma and CRSwNP, has a body of evidence supporting advancement into Phase 3 in both diseases. In the Phase 2 VALIANT trial, 100 mg every 12 weeks reduced the annualized asthma exacerbation rate by 56% vs placebo.

items.title: Air Pollution Reprograms Brain Immune Cells, Raises Dementia Risk by 25%
items.summary: A translational study in the Journal of Neuroinflammation by Case Western Reserve University and partners reports that fine particulate (PM2.5) exposure is associated with a 25% higher dementia risk and reshapes microglial programs. Higher pollution raised dementia risk regardless of inherited Alzheimer's genetic risk.

items.title: Only 13% of Lung Cancer Patients Would Have Qualified for Advance Screening Based on Eligibility Guidelines
items.publisher: Elsevier (Journal of the American College of Radiology)
items.summary: An analysis of 1,119 patients aged 50-80 diagnosed with lung cancer in a Southern California health system found only 13% would have qualified for screening under eligibility guidelines. Authors also found smoking history in medical records was often too incomplete to determine eligibility.

items.title: Who Gets Screened for Lung Cancer? Northwestern Medicine Researchers Say it's Time to Rethink the Answer
items.summary: Northwestern Medicine is studying universal, age-based lung cancer screening, noting earlier research found only 35% of its lung cancer patients would have met USPSTF criteria. In its screening study, 40% of participants with smoking history were ineligible under current criteria and six early-stage cancers were detected and treated, including two stage 1 cancers in never-smokers.
